sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in Lakewood, NJ?
sections.html:
Lakewood is a flat, fast-growing township in Ocean County, and a house here moves through township code enforcement, an Ocean County recording office and a state fee schedule before the deed changes hands. You can list with an agent, sell on your own, or accept an as-is cash purchase, and each path ends at the same three desks.

Lakewood covers 24.68 square miles of land and is the most populous township in Ocean County. The 2025 Census estimate is 143,765 residents, up from 135,158 in the 2020 count. Households here average 4.36 people, so floor plan and bedroom count weigh heavily when a buyer looks at a house.

sections.h2: How has Lakewood grown, and what does the land look like?
sections.html:
Lakewood began as a sawmill and bog-iron area in the 1700s. It was called Bricksburg in 1865, renamed Lakewood in 1880 as a winter resort, and incorporated as a township on March 23, 1892, from part of Brick Township. In the 1960s much of the woods and cranberry bogs gave way to subdivisions, and Leisure Village opened for sale in 1963.

The township sits on the coastal plain, mostly 20 to 80 feet above sea level. The North Branch of the Metedeconk River forms part of the northern and eastern edge, and four man-made lakes (Carasaljo, Manetta, Shenandoah and Waddill) shape several neighborhoods. Greenville, Seven Stars, South Lakewood and Lake Carasaljo are place names you will see on listings. The township touches Brick, Jackson, Toms River and Howell.

The Census counts the Lakewood area as a CDP of 69,398 people in 2020, with the age-restricted Leisure Village and Leisure Village East communities counted separately at 4,966 and 4,189. If your house is in one of those communities, ask the association for its resale rules before you sign anything.

sections.h2: What do Lakewood housing numbers look like?
sections.html:
Lakewood households are large. The Census reports 4.36 people per household, and 51.5% of homes are owner-occupied. Median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $466,700.

A median household income near $65,000 beside a $466,700 median home value means many buyers lean on mortgages, family money or cash. That is one reason as-is offers are common on tired or oddly laid-out houses here.

sections.h2: Which employers and institutions shape Lakewood's economy?
sections.html:
Education and health care lead. Census figures put 2022 health care and social assistance receipts at about $1.54 billion and retail sales at about $3.25 billion. Beth Medrash Govoha, founded in 1943, is the largest yeshiva outside Israel, and Georgian Court University has sat on Lake Carasaljo since 1924.

Part of the township was a state Urban Enterprise Zone from 1994, and that status expired in October 2025. The zone helped fund ShoreTown Ballpark, the 6,588-seat home of the Jersey Shore BlueClaws. If a buyer asks about sales-tax treatment of nearby stores, point them to the township instead of guessing.

sections.h2: What schools and commuting routes affect resale value?
sections.html:
The Lakewood School District runs eight schools with 5,433 students in the 2021-22 school year, and the district also buses students to private schools, which reached about 25,000 students at yeshivas and other schools by 2016. Many families choose a home by walking distance to a yeshiva or school rather than by the public school zone, so ask your agent which side of a street a buyer would prefer.

Getting around is straightforward by car and bus. These are the main links buyers ask about:

  • Garden State Parkway exit 89, which also feeds Route 70 after exit 88 closed permanently in November 2014.
  • Route 70, Route 88 and Route 9, plus county roads 526, 528, 547 and 549.
  • The Lakewood Bus Terminal, where NJ Transit runs routes 137 and 139 to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, route 317 to Philadelphia, route 67 to Newark and route 559 to Atlantic City.
  • The in-town Lakewood Shuttle and Ocean Ride routes OC3 and OC4.

sections.h2: What does Lakewood's code enforcement office require before a sale?
sections.html:
Start with the Township of Lakewood's Code Enforcement office at 212 4th Street, phone 732-364-3760. Its rental and housing window runs 8:30 AM to 4 PM, and its page carries a legal notice to residential property owners about smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. Ask the staff what resale paperwork and inspection your closing date needs, and request the form list in writing.

The township's FAQ also lists a question on whether a certificate of occupancy is needed when selling a home. Confirm the current answer by phone before you schedule a closing. Also ask about open permits, because the office states that work done without a required permit can bring a penalty of up to $2,000, plus $2,000 for each week the violation stays open.

  • Permit review under the state construction code can take up to 20 business days.
  • The engineering section of the township FAQ covers flood zone lookups and elevation certificates, property surveys and wetlands questions.
  • Rental houses need a separate rental certificate of occupancy application before a new tenant moves in.

sections.h2: Where is the deed recorded and what fees apply in Lakewood?
sections.html:
Deeds for Lakewood go to the Ocean County Clerk. The main office is at 118 Washington Street in Toms River, phone (732) 929-2018, open Monday to Friday 8 AM to 4:30 PM with in-person service until 4 PM. The clerk's contact page also lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, phone (732) 370-8850.

The state's realty transfer fee falls on the seller. Because Lakewood's median home value of $466,700 is above $350,000, the higher schedule applies: $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000, $4.25 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000, and $4.80 per $500 from $200,000 to $550,000. Above $1 million a graduated percent fee of 1% to 3.5% is added and the seller pays it as well.

If you owe back taxes, ask the Lakewood tax collector for a payoff figure. The township advertised an online sale of 2025 and prior-year delinquent taxes and water or sewer charges with a sale date of October 28, 2026, so accounts that were not redeemed may carry a certificate now.

sections.h2: Should I list, sell on my own, or take a cash offer in Lakewood?
sections.html:
Choose by timeline and condition. A listing reaches the most buyers but brings showings, a lender appraisal and a township inspection step. A sale on your own saves the commission and puts the paperwork on you. An as-is cash purchase removes repairs and financing risk, but you should compare the written terms, including who pays the transfer fee and who orders any township certificate.

Whatever you pick, gather the survey, any open permit records, tenant leases if the house is rented, and the latest tax bill. Buyers in Lakewood move fast when the paperwork is clean, and they walk when a permit or an occupancy question surfaces late.

faqs.q: Does Lakewood require an inspection before I sell my house?
faqs.a: Ask the township. Code Enforcement at 732-364-3760 handles smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules and resale paperwork, and its FAQ lists a certificate of occupancy question for home sellers. Confirm the exact requirement for your address before you set a closing date.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Lakewood sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The state charges it on the deed price when the Ocean County Clerk records the deed, and sales above $1 million also carry a graduated percent fee that falls on the seller.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed for a Lakewood house?
faqs.a: Record it with the Ocean County Clerk, 118 Washington Street, Toms River, phone (732) 929-2018. The clerk also lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, phone (732) 370-8850.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lakewood house with open permits or code violations?
faqs.a: Yes, but resolve or disclose them first. Code Enforcement can tell you which permits are open, and unpermitted work can draw a penalty of up to $2,000 plus $2,000 for each week it stays open. A buyer or lender may require the permit closed before closing.

faqs.q: How does a cash sale differ from listing in Lakewood?
faqs.a: A cash sale usually skips repairs, appraisal and mortgage approval, so it can close sooner. A listing may reach more buyers. In both cases the deed recording, transfer fee and any township certificate still apply, so compare the written terms.
